focus.text: English has three ways of writing about now, and each one tells your reader something different. The simple present is for facts and routines that do not change. The present progressive is for what is happening now or around now, so it suggests something temporary. The present perfect connects an earlier action to the present moment, which is why it works so well for experience and for change. Choosing carefully between them is often the difference between a sentence the reader trusts and one they have to read twice.

summaryTable.caption: The three present forms at a glance
rows: He **is saving** for a new laptop.
past action that still matters now
He **has saved** two million đồng so far.

pretest.sentence: Mai usually revises in the library after class.
pretest.reason: A routine takes the simple present, and *usually* sits before the main verb.

pretest.sentence: My cousin study economics in Hồ Chí Minh City.
pretest.reason: A third-person singular subject (*my cousin*) needs *studies*.

pretest.sentence: This street very noisy in the evening.
pretest.reason: An adjective cannot be the verb: write *This street **is** very noisy*.

pretest.sentence: At the moment I am writing a report about air quality.
pretest.reason: *At the moment* points to right now, so the present progressive is right.

pretest.sentence: I am knowing the answer to this question.
pretest.reason: *know* is a stative verb, so use the simple present: *I know*.

pretest.sentence: She has lived in Đà Nẵng since 2019.
pretest.reason: An action that started in the past and continues now takes the present perfect with *since*.

pretest.sentence: I live here since last April.
pretest.reason: With *since*, use the present perfect: *I have lived here since last April*.

pretest.sentence: We have been waiting for the results for three weeks.
pretest.reason: The present perfect progressive stresses how long an unfinished action has been going on.

pretest.sentence: He has finished his homework yesterday.
pretest.reason: A finished time word (*yesterday*) needs the simple past: *He finished*.

pretest.sentence: My laptop is belonging to my sister.
pretest.reason: *belong* describes a state, so it stays simple: *My laptop belongs to my sister*.

context.title: A week in a student's life
context.paragraph: Linh studies at a high school in Cầu Giấy, and her week rarely changes. She leaves home at half past six, because the traffic gets heavy after seven. This month she is preparing for a speaking test, so she practises with a classmate every Thursday evening. She has recorded eight of those conversations already, and she says the recordings show how much her pronunciation has improved. Her teacher believes that steady practice matters more than talent. Right now Linh is reading an article about air quality in Hà Nội, and she has decided to use it in her next essay.

sections.title: Forming the simple present

table.caption: Simple present: statements, negatives and questions

timeline.label: Repeated action: it happened before now, it happens now, and it will happen again.

notes: Add **-es** after -ch, -sh, -s, -x and -z (*teaches, washes, misses, fixes, buzzes*). If the verb ends in a consonant + **y**, change the y to **-ies** (*study → studies*), but keep the y after a vowel (*play → plays*).

items.stem: My brother ___ in a coffee shop at the weekend.
items.reason: *My brother* is he, so the verb takes -s.

items.stem: She ___ English every morning before school.
items.reason: Consonant + y becomes -ies in the third person singular.

items.stem: The bus ___ not stop outside our school.
items.reason: *The bus* is it, so the negative uses *does not*.

items.stem: ___ your parents work in the city centre?
items.reason: *Your parents* is plural, so the question starts with *Do*.

sections.title: Using the simple present

rules.text: Use the simple present for facts and things that stay true.

examples.text: Hà Nội **has** four seasons, and the summer **is** long.

rules.text: Use it for routines and habits, often with a frequency adverb (*always, usually, often, rarely, never*) before the main verb.

examples.text: Tuấn **always checks** the weather before he cycles to work.
We **rarely eat** out during the week.

rules.text: Use it to give an opinion or to report what a text says, which is why it is common in essays.

examples.text: The chart **shows** that rents **rise** every year.
Many people **believe** that public transport **needs** more investment.

tips: In IELTS Writing Task 1, describe what a chart shows in the simple present: *the graph shows*, *the figure represents*. Save the past tense for the years the data covers.

sections.title: Forming the present progressive and the present perfect
notes: Spelling of -ing: drop a silent **e** (*write → writing*), and double a final consonant after a single stressed vowel (*plan → planning*, *begin → beginning*).

items.reason: The action is happening right now, so use the present progressive.

items.stem: My father ___ for the same company since 2010.
items.reason: *since 2010* links the past to now, so the present perfect is correct.
*understand* is stative, so it stays in the simple present.
A finished number of actions inside an unfinished period takes the present perfect.

items.stem: This week the students ___ their presentations.
items.reason: *This week* frames a temporary period around now.

sections.title: Using the present progressive and the present perfect

rules.text: Use the present progressive for an action in progress now, or for a temporary situation around now.

examples.text: I **am writing** to ask about your summer course.
Prices **are rising** faster than wages this year.

rules.text: Use the present perfect when the time is not finished, or when the result still matters now.

examples.text: She **has visited** three provinces this month.
The city **has banned** plastic bags, so shops now use paper ones.

rules.text: Keep stative verbs (*know, believe, own, belong, contain, prefer*) in the simple present, even when you mean right now.

tips: *Have been to* means you went and came back; *have gone to* means you are still there. In an essay about your own experience, you almost always want *have been to*.

sections.title: Using the present perfect progressive

timeline.label: An action that started earlier, has continued, and is still going on now.

rules.text: Use *have / has been + verb-ing* to stress how long an unfinished action has lasted, usually with *for* or *since*.

examples.text: They **have been collecting** plastic waste since March.
I **have been revising** for two hours and I need a break.

rules.text: Prefer the present perfect (not the progressive) when you count finished results.

examples.text: She **has been writing** all afternoon. (how long)

rules.text: Match the time word to the form: *every day, usually* → simple present; *now, at the moment, this week* → present progressive; *since, for, already, yet, so far* → present perfect.

examples.text: So far the club **has recruited** twenty members.
At the moment we **are testing** the new design.

notes: Stative verbs have no progressive form, so *have known* — never *have been knowing* — is the way to say how long you have known someone.

items.sentence: I have been knowing Trang since primary school.
items.reason: *know* is stative, so it has no progressive form.

items.sentence: We have visited the museum last weekend.
items.reason: *last weekend* is finished time, so use the simple past.

items.sentence: My sister work at a hospital in Huế.
This room very cold in winter.
items.reason: The sentence has no verb; an adjective needs *be*.

items.sentence: I am agree with the writer's main point.
items.reason: *agree* is already a verb, so it does not take *be*.

editing.text: My name is Quân and I am student at a high school in Cần Thơ. Every morning I take the bus to school, and my best friend Hải usually wait for me at the stop. This term we are prepare for the national English competition, so we practise together twice a week. I am knowing that the reading part is my weakness, so I have started a vocabulary notebook in September. So far I have wrote more than two hundred words in it. My teacher says that the notebook help students remember new language, and she is right. This morning I review it on the bus, and I remembered almost everything.

errors.reason: A singular count noun needs an article.
*Hải* is he, so the verb takes -s.
*know* is stative, so it stays in the simple present.

errors.span: have started a vocabulary notebook in September
errors.fix: started a vocabulary notebook in September
errors.reason: *in September* is a finished time, so use the simple past.
The present perfect uses the past participle *written*.
*The notebook* is it, so the verb takes -s.
The rest of the sentence is past (*remembered*), so keep one time frame.

topics.prompt: Write an email to an exchange student who is coming to your school next month. Describe what a normal school day looks like and what your class is doing this term.
checklist: Routines are in the simple present, with frequency adverbs before the main verb.
At least two sentences use the present progressive for this term's temporary activities.
Every third-person singular verb ends in -s.

topics.prompt: Describe how your study habits have changed since you started secondary school. Say what you have tried and what you are still working on.
checklist: Changes that still matter now use the present perfect.
Finished times (*last year*, *in 2023*) use the simple past, not the present perfect.
At least one sentence uses *since* or *for* with the present perfect.

topics.prompt: Your class is running a project to reduce plastic waste. Write a short progress report for your teacher: what the group does every week, what it is doing now, and what it has achieved so far.
checklist: The report mixes all three present forms, each for its own purpose.
Results so far are counted with the present perfect (*we have collected…*).
No stative verb appears in the -ing form.
